comments.text:
Date: Monday, September 21, 2026
Vehicle/System: Chuter 62 Healey — Ampere EV VCU (New Eagle VCM_519), single motor, direct drive
Firmware: DiagCANSW 1.8.13 / build 516 → 1.9.3 / build 519 (VCM_519_RC010903_Persist)
ClickUp: Checkout Vehicle — Monthly Goal, Chuter 62 Healey · Open · High · due Sep 30 · 22.5 h logged
Objective
Bring Chuter onto the same 1.9.3 firmware as the Blazers, update and reconfigure the GUI, identify every calibration the flash changed, restore the shop's settings, and secure delivery backups.
What we did
Confirmed with Marc that Chuter goes to the same build as the Blazers. Updated and reconfigured the GUI, captured a pre-flash screenshot set, flashed to 1.9.3 / build 519, and captured a matching post-flash set. Ran a field-by-field comparison, applied all the restores, then revised the per-mode torque limits after talking it through with Marc. Uploaded EEPROM and PMU project files to the Drive as delivery backups.
Key findings
Seven calibrations changed, and all seven are live. Drive mode on this car reads Normal, so unlike Preheim there's no AWD tab absorbing the resets — everything the flash touched landed on tables Chuter actually uses.

undefined
The torque-limit wipe was the one that mattered most. The pedal maps already reach 100%, so the per-mode multiplier is the peak torque limit — at 100/100/100 there was effectively no limit in any mode. Launch gain is now a single value in 1.9.3 rather than a table, so that restore was one entry.
Per-mode torque limits are intentionally back at 100 / 100 / 100. They were initially set to 50 / 75 / 100, but those were Preheim's numbers, not Healey's — Chuter's own pre-flash values were never captured and aren't on the 1.8.13 Config tab. After talking with Marc, reverted deliberately to 100 across Eco, Normal and Sport.
Chuter was already close to the new defaults. Most of what 1.9.3 installs as defaults, this car was already running pre-flash — which is why only seven values moved, versus ten on Ritchie. Six new blocks came in sitting at flash defaults.
All seven restores verified against post-adjustment screenshots; every row of the comparison now carries pre-flash, post-flash and current values.
Seventeen tabs are unverified — no screenshot on either side of the flash, so nothing was compared on them.
Prior work on this checkout
Aug 12 (Devin) — Restored inverter firmware and settings, verified gamma adjust, reviewed the checkout sheet, updated VCU firmware to 1.8.14 for the torque tuning mods, uploaded backups.
Aug 24 — Set vehicle parameters to calibration: wheel diameter 0.660 → 0.649 m, gear ratio 4.300 → 6.726, weight 1500 → 1263 kg. Verified persistence through a key cycle. Corrected the gear ratio after Dan's Healey ratio was entered by mistake. Client wifi credentials collected and loaded by Devin. Heater finding: this car's heater circuit is wired to the older standard — blower motor and heater contactor triggered by the same switch off one PDU output. Upper management signed off as acceptable; the proper fix would move the contactor positive lead to the "AC Blower" positive in the HVAC sub so the heater can't energize without blower load. Works as built.
Aug 25 — Held, waiting for the vehicle to be driven down to ≤10% SOC.
Artifacts produced
Pre-flash (5) and post-flash (5) screenshot sets, plus six adjustment captures — on the ClickUp goal
Field-by-field pre/post/current comparison
EEPROM and PMU project files uploaded to the Drive — flagged to the channel as the only backups for these two, since neither is reported in the VCU log. Any change has to be documented and the Drive files replaced.

comments.text:
Date: Wednesday, September 23, 2026
Vehicle/System: Chuter 62 Healey — Ampere EV VCU (New Eagle VCM_519), single motor, direct drive
Firmware: VCM_519_RC010903_Persist (1.9.3 / build 519) → VCM_515_RC010813_ENone (build 515)
ClickUp: Checkout Vehicle — Monthly Goal, Chuter 62 Healey · Open · High · due Sep 30
Objective
Diagnose the drive-loss and cut-out events that appeared on the delivery run to Colvin's, and get the car back to a known-good state.
What happened
The car finished charging overnight and was staged for delivery. On the run to Colvin's, Ryan lost throttle twice when lifting off to come to a stop, each time with a coinciding clunk. Turning regen off appeared to stop it. Near Colvin's the car cut off while accelerating from a stop — hard cut, loud clunk. It cut off once more at a stoplight on the way back, no noise, and the motor was cogging intermittently at stoplights and in traffic. Justin noted he'd had something similar taking Alvarez to Colvin's, outcome not remembered.
Key findings
The fault is real and it lives in regen. Two logs captured back to back — regen on and regen off. The regen-off drive was harder on the drive system and never faulted; the regen-on log shows a genuine inverter trip. So this is not a general current or thermal problem — it only shows up under deep negative torque.
The trip, in detail (regen-on log, 12:44):
Going in, everything is clean. At ~104 s, lift-off at ~2,250 rpm (40 mph), no brake. The VCM ramps regen smoothly to its −104.8 Nm ceiling and the motor follows it well: −97 to −100 Nm actual, battery taking about −47 A, 64 A at peak.
The trip: at 108.0 s, 1,555 rpm (28 mph), the inverter drops out. Torque and current go to zero in a single sample. The VCM sets DrvInvtrFault, and after its 2 s debounce logs InvtrReportsOverCurrentFault and InvtrReportsGenFault. DrvMtrTrqLo follows as a side effect.
Nothing else looks wrong. Bus voltage peaks at 394.8 V, motor/inverter temps 52/61 °C, BMS fine, CAN message ages normal. There's a modest ~100 rpm dip and a −112 Nm overshoot at 106.4 s, but the sample rate is too low to call that a cause.
It latches. The fault holds for the rest of the log (to 142.7 s). Neutral-and-back-to-Drive doesn't clear it; the car makes no torque even with 98 Nm requested. Only a key cycle clears it.
Threshold behavior: the deepest regen before this event was about −80 Nm at up to ~1,270 rpm (~22 mph), and that was fine. The trip came on the first push past that, at higher speed.
Motoring and regen efficiency measured at the battery look identical in both logs, so nothing in the data points to a sensor or resolver-angle problem.
Correction to Monday's baseline: the car was on 515, not 516. Double-checking the before photos showed the pre-flash firmware was actually VCM_515_RC010813_ENone, so the revert target was one step further back than recorded.
The revert fixed it. Back on 515, the car returned to normal operating conditions. The off-throttle pedal delay is gone and regen never faulted the inverter — multiple hard pedal stabs and the car could not be made to fault or feel strange in any way.
Open disagreement on cause. Marc's read is that this doesn't look like a VCU issue and points to inverter firmware. Inverter firmware wasn't touched Monday, and old backups can be compared against the most recent to confirm. Marc last drove the car on the highway Friday morning 9/18 and it was perfect — the only two changes since are the VCU firmware upgrade and a full overnight charge.
Next steps
Recharge to full and retest on 515 — in progress. Being at the top of the pack is the other variable that changed, and the regen ceiling is highest there.
Compare old vs. most recent inverter firmware backups to close out Marc's theory.
Verify every setting re-entered correctly after the revert.
Decide the path forward on 1.9.3 — whether this is a regen calibration ceiling that needs lowering on this car, or a genuine firmware incompatibility.
Re-plan delivery — the Colvin's drop-off did not complete.
Status
Car is back on 515 and behaving normally. Delivery is on hold. Root cause not yet established: the symptom tracks the VCU firmware change, but the fault is reported by the inverter under deep regen only, and Marc's inverter-firmware theory is still open. Recharging now for the confirming test at full pack.

EOD — 16 Sep 2026 — Lee & Kelly test pull analysis
Done today
Compared inverter EEPROM dumps: Kelly (SN 958) vs Lee (SN 1469). Only 4 of 101 shared params differ — serial, gamma (32.9° vs 34.7°), relay output state (12 vs 0), torque rate limit (5.0 vs 7.0 Nm). Brake_Lo missing from the Lee dump, likely a capture artifact, needs a re-pull to confirm.
Built a 117-signal list valid on both VCU display tabs (VCM_490 and VCM_517) for motor-behavior comparison.
Analyzed both cars' Motoring Diag test pulls. Three reports issued: Lee, Kelly, and a Lee-vs-Kelly comparison.
Main finding — affects both cars
 Both VCUs command 580 Nm; both inverters deliver ~460 Nm from ~1400 rpm up. ~130 Nm short. Not a derate — no faults, cold, no thermal or voltage limit. Both carry DrvInvtrMCL = 1272 A, matching IQ_Limit_EEPROM 12720 on both dumps. The current limit binds before the torque limit. Every VCU and inverter limit is identical across the two cars, so this is one shared decision, not a per-car calibration issue. Do not raise the current limit without checking motor/inverter ratings and pack discharge capability first — lowering the request may be the right fix.
Kelly-specific — needs resolving before her numbers can be trusted
 Reported shaft power exceeds measured DC input power in 31% of full-throttle samples, peaking at 2.04×. Physically impossible. Present in both pulls (27.7% and 33.4%). Lee never crosses 1.0. Pack current vs inverter DC current disagree by up to 264 A — and it's worse in pull 2 (sd 60 A) than pull 1 (sd 18 A), so it looks intermittent. Start with the pack current path: IVT/BMS message rate, message age, stale holds. Kelly's Gamma_Adjust reading 329 is a secondary lead on the torque estimate, unconfirmed.
Cars are otherwise near-identical
 Delivered torque within 6 Nm from 2000–5000 rpm. Gearing within 0.7%. 20→60 mph: Lee 4.02 s, Kelly 3.95 s.

Kelly / Lee — EOD, Wed 17 Sep
Display tab rebuilt. Stripped the Motoring Diag tab from 117 columns to 51 and renamed it Motoring Claude. Removed 23 calibration boxes and 29 dead constants; added five reason codes and four message-age channels. Result: clean 100 ms logging with zero cal-read gaps, against 5,300+ gaps over 50 ms before. Full channel spec is in the Motoring Diag Tab document.
Three full-throttle pulls on Kelly with the new pedal (13:58 session, two pulls; 14:07 session, one).
New pedal is confirmed good. Both sensors correlate 0.99997, ADC ratio holds 2.0218 ± 0.0059, pedal wobble 0.37% RMS at full throttle. It also cut the high-speed current ripple roughly in half and moved its onset from 50 mph to 60 mph. Replicated on all three pulls.
Found the cause of the high-speed torque taper. DrvMtrTrqLim — the VCU's own torque ceiling — holds 580 Nm to 60 mph, then falls to ~500 Nm by 65 and ~440 by 75. Delivered torque follows it down. That ceiling works out to a near-constant 345–355 kW of shaft power, so it's a calibration choice, not hardware. The inverter's actual power limit reads 395 kW and the car only ever drew 317 kW.
But there's a second, separate problem underneath it. At every speed on every pull, the car delivers 85–132 Nm less than its own declared ceiling. Below 60 mph the ceiling is a flat 580 Nm and the car makes 450–465. Nothing in the log accounts for it. This is the shortfall we've been chasing since Tuesday, now cleanly separated from the taper.
The DC power ripple is not commanded. Pedal and torque command are flat to within 0.5% while inverter current swings 8–9%. The ripple is real — bus voltage responds at 54–73 mΩ against the pack's measured 80.6 mΩ — but it produces no torque: reported torque swings eight times less and correlates negatively with current. That's the signature of field-weakening (d-axis) current hunting, and it starts at the same 58–60 mph where the torque ceiling begins tapering.
Everything still points at rotor angle on Kelly. One error would explain all three symptoms: the torque estimate reading high (shaft power still exceeds DC input on 41–56% of samples), the field-weakening regulator hunting, and the speed-dependent ripple. Gamma_Adjust_EEPROM reads 329 on Kelly against 347 on Lee.
Three things I got wrong earlier today and have retracted:
The "current channel split above 75 mph" was noise. Two more pulls give +11 A and −19 A — the sign flips. It was measurement phase at 10 Hz, not a real disagreement.
The "constant power wall at 288 kW" had the causation backwards. Torque is capped; flat power is the consequence.
AmpereBMSPeak_Discharge_Current is not a limit. It rises monotonically from 3 A to 589 A and never falls — it's a peak recorder.
Also worth noting: the BMS current message goes stale at a standstill, freezing the pack-current reading on 12.7% of samples (31.6% while stationary, 1.2% above 40 mph). It never touched a full-throttle sample, but idle and creep current data from Kelly shouldn't be trusted.

comments.author: Brandon Beaman
comments.text:
Test drove vehicle.
Found that the vehicle makes much more torque now. Enough to finally chirp the tires a little bit.
However when the tires break traction the inverter has faulted out both times.
Two events, both a complete loss of drive


During both, inverter current sits at 0.2–0.4 A and delivered torque at zero. The car is making nothing for forty seconds at a stretch.
In event 2 the driver clearly tried to get it back — at t = 355.6 to 356.4 the pedal goes 68%, 81%, 97%, command rises to 350 Nm, and the inverter still puts out 0.2 A.

Both trip at the same place

Both faults set on the very next sample after peak torque, during a hard launch from low speed.
It isn't torque on its own. Pull 2 made 591 Nm at 4,746 rpm and pull 3 made 589 Nm at 3,148 rpm, and neither tripped. Both trips were below 1,750 rpm. The envelope that kills it is high torque below about 2,000 rpm — which is exactly where phase current peaks and back-EMF is lowest, even though DC current is only ~200 A. With IQ_Limit_EEPROM at 1272 A, that corner is where the phase-current limit would bite first.
Not thermal: inverter was at 42–44 °C and the motor at 24–40 °C at both trips. Stone cold.

Neither clears on its own
Both events end only when HV is cycled. Bus goes 590 → 260 → 33 → 0 V, validity flags drop for 8 s (event 1) and 3.8 s (event 2), HV comes back, fault clears. Nothing in the log suggests it would have recovered otherwise.

Nothing else flags it
DrvInvtrDsblReason reads No Fault on all 11,582 samples. So do APPLimReason, LimpInModeReason and both HVSysDsblLevel codes. DrvMtrTrqVld and DrvInvtrCurVld stay at 1 throughout the fault — they only drop during the HV-off window. The raw DrvInvtrFault bit is the only thing that catches this, which is worth knowing for the tab spec and for anyone reading these logs.

comments.text:
Further diag / analysis on Lee for the inverter fault.
Shows that the inverter is faulting due to an over current. However it does also seem like there might be a potential phase irregularity. coming through when the torque is peaked and or when the tire break traction.
Will need to reach out to cascadia on this one as per Marcs request.
We did get the full torque back though now so there is definitely an issue with the newest 6533 firmware thats knocking 100+Nm off of our max usable torque.
Attached is a sort report based on the EEPROM, Inverter Diag Data and a Raptor log. This report however is not a concrete problem nor a solution but a general report based on the diag data we I collected. Using my claude.


Date: Tuesday, September 22, 2026
Vehicle/System: Lee 68 Mustang — Cascadia inverter, Ampere EV VCU (New Eagle VCM_517)
Inverter firmware: GEN5_CC_CM_20250514_6533 (defsyms_20250513) → GEN5_CC_CM_20240829_6531 (defsyms_20240829)
ClickUp: Checkout vehicle — Monthly Goal, Lee 68 Mustang · Open · Urgent · due Sep 30 · 2.5 h of 8 h logged (5.5 h remaining)
Objective
Back-rev the Cascadia inverter to 6531 to recover the missing peak torque, verify no EEPROM configuration was lost in the revert, and road-test to confirm the vehicle now makes full requested torque.
What we did
Confirmed the target build with Marc and Devin before flashing. Reverted the inverter from 6533 to 6531, then ran a before/after EEPROM comparison to prove nothing live was lost. Road-tested with full-throttle pulls, captured Raptor logs, and analyzed the two inverter faults that came out of it. Added signals to the 10 ms log list, set shudder compensation back to stock per Marc, and pulled inverter diag data and the full EEPROM for Cascadia.
Key findings
The back-rev worked — torque is back. The car now makes 100% of requested torque, and arguably 102%. It makes enough torque to chirp the tires, which it could not do on 6533.
The revert cost nothing live. All EEPROM settings stayed persistent through the flash. Only four parameters disappear on 6531 — the Active Short Circuit trio and the DC-link flux-weakening flag — and all four were reading zero on 6533, so no live configuration was lost. Documented in Lee_Mustang_Firmware_Revert_Verification.pdf.
New problem: the inverter faults when the tires break traction. Two events on the first drive, both a complete loss of drive. During both, inverter current sits at 0.2–0.4 A with delivered torque at zero — the car makes nothing for forty seconds at a stretch. In event 2 the driver clearly tried to get it back: at t = 355.6–356.4 s the pedal goes 68% → 81% → 97% and command rises to 350 Nm, and the inverter still puts out 0.2 A.
Both trip in the same envelope, and it isn't torque alone. Both faults set on the very next sample after peak torque, during a hard launch from low speed, both below 1,750 rpm. Pull 2 made 591 Nm at 4,746 rpm and pull 3 made 589 Nm at 3,148 rpm — neither tripped. The envelope that kills it is high torque below about 2,000 rpm, exactly where phase current peaks and back-EMF is lowest, even though DC current is only ~200 A. With IQ_Limit_EEPROM at 1272 A, that corner is where the phase-current limit would bite first.
Not thermal. Inverter at 42–44 °C and motor at 24–40 °C at both trips. Stone cold.
Neither clears on its own. Both events end only when HV is cycled: bus goes 590 → 260 → 33 → 0 V, validity flags drop for 8 s (event 1) and 3.8 s (event 2), HV comes back, fault clears. Nothing in the log suggests it would have recovered otherwise.
Nothing but the raw bit catches it. DrvInvtrDsblReason reads No Fault on all 11,582 samples — as do APPLimReason, LimpInModeReason and both HVSysDsblLevel codes. DrvMtrTrqVld and DrvInvtrCurVld stay at 1 throughout the fault and only drop during the HV-off window. The raw DrvInvtrFault bit is the only signal that catches this — worth knowing for the tab spec and for anyone else reading these logs.
Fault decoded as hardware over-current. Marc read it out as INV_Run_Fault_Lo = 0x0200 (Post faults both 0x0000) — Hardware Over-current Fault, 0x00000200. Raptor surfaces it as InvtrReportsOverCurrentFault. Devin's read on the trace was that CAN1 may have dropped.
On the version question: Marc flagged a possible 6532 between the two builds; Devin confirmed 6532 was skipped — 6531 is the right target. Devin also noted some inverters have arrived from the factory on that firmware, and he had to fabricate a symbols file to pull an EEPROM backup before flashing; that extracted firmware is overwritten now.

comments.author: Brandon Beaman
comments.text:
This is with the Torque rate set back to 50. No real change there.

Wasn't able to get diag data. RMS GUI wouldn't open. Diving into that next. Could be indicator to a damaged harness if I cant get this setup to work on another vehicle.

Here a couple claude responses.

Q: Could this be drivetrain?
Drivetrain momentum is probably what sets it off, but it can't be what the resolver is reading. The logs show both effects, and they differ by a factor of about 40.
Real driveline motion is slow. In the 10 ms log, the motor speed rings after the trip as the driveline unwinds:
It drops from 1,632 to 1,516 rpm, back up to 1,709 rpm, and keeps ringing about every 140 ms.
That's a swing of about ±100 rpm at roughly 7 Hz, the driveline winding up and springing back once the torque disappears.
The current loop copes easily with a speed change that slow and small.
The resolver disturbance is far faster and far bigger:
It swings at about 300 Hz.
In a fraction of a millisecond, the resolver reports the speed dropping to about a quarter of 1,650 rpm, then doubling, then briefly reversing.
For the rotor to really do that, it would need well over 10,000 Nm acting on it. The motor makes 580 Nm. Even a hard shock from the tires hooking back up can't come close to that at the rotor without breaking something. So the rotor isn't moving the way the resolver says.


Q: Could this be Torque Rate Limit?
Probably not. The rate limit only slows down how fast the torque command can change. At the trip the command wasn't changing, and the ramps in the logs never reached either limit.
What the setting means. Cascadia's software manual defines Torque_Rate_Limit_EEPROM as torque increase per 3 ms:
SettingPer 3 msPer secondOld: 505 Nmabout 1,670 Nm/sNow: 707 Nmabout 2,330 Nm/s
Cascadia only warns about stability above 70 Nm per 3 ms (a setting of 700, about 23,000 Nm/s). Lee's 7 Nm is a tenth of that.
Why it isn't causing the trip:
The command was flat when it tripped. In the diag file the current commands (Iq_cmd / Id_cmd) held steady for the whole 26.7 ms before the trip. A rate limiter only acts while the command is rising or falling, so it had nothing to do. The current ran away while the command sat still, the same point that rules out shudder compensation.
The trips didn't ramp as fast as the limit allows. The steepest actual torque rise in each pull, from the logs:
PullSteepest torque riseTrip 1~1,700 Nm/sTrip 2~1,500 Nm/sTrip 3~700 Nm/sClean rolling pull~2,280 Nm/s
The pedal and the VCU's own ramp set these rates, not the inverter setting. Even at the old 5 Nm limit, trips 2 and 3 would have ramped the same way.
The fastest ramp didn't trip. The clean rolling pull came right up against the 7 Nm limit and ran fine. All three trips ramped slower.


Q: Could the Gamma be affected with a new cable?
Not if the new cable is wired pin for pin the same. Gamma adjust corrects for where the resolver sits on the shaft relative to the rotor magnets. Cascadia's software manual describes it as compensating for the resolver's position on the shaft. A cable swap doesn't move anything mechanically, so the offset shouldn't change.
Verify after the swap:
Direction: with the motor stopped, turn the shaft slowly by hand in the forward direction.
Gamma_Resolver should count up and wrap from 360° to 0.
Sin_corr and Cos_corr should trace a circle.
If the angle counts down or doesn't move, a pair is swapped or reversed. That shows up as a 90° or 180° error, or the motor won't run at all, not a small drift.
Offset check: coast the motor down with the inverter disabled and read Delta_Resolver_In_Fil. It should read +90° forward (or −90° in reverse), within ±0.7°.
If it's within that, leave Gamma_Adjust at 34.7°.
If it's outside that, redo the calibration per section 4.1.3 of the manual.
Spinning the motor generates HV even with the inverter off, so follow the manual's precautions.
If the new cable is a different length or type: it can delay the resolver signals relative to the excitation. That doesn't shift the angle, because sin and cos are delayed equally. It does lower the signal amplitude the inverter reads, which makes it more sensitive to noise. Cascadia has a Resolver PWM Delay setting that tunes when the inverter samples the resolver signal (default 1100). Look at the sin/cos amplitude after the swap, and ask Cascadia before changing that setting.
